passage:
Dear Madhuri didi,
I need to tell someone, and you're the only one who won't laugh.
At lunch the girls in my group were making fun of the new boy's accent. Kritika did an imitation and everyone cracked up. I laughed too. I didn't think it was funny at all. I felt sick. He was sitting two tables away.
Then they asked if the school trip should be to the water park instead of the science museum. I actually really wanted the museum. I said, "Water park, obviously."
I keep doing this. I agree with whatever they say and laugh at whatever they laugh at, because if I don't, what if they stop saving me a seat?
Is this normal? It doesn't feel like me.
Love,
Vandana

qa.q: What did Vandana say about the school trip?
qa.a: Vandana said, "Water park, obviously," despite really wanting the museum.

qa.q: What is Vandana afraid will happen if Vandana disagrees with the group?
qa.a: Vandana fears they will stop saving a seat, so fitting in feels more important than honest opinions or feelings.

qa.q: What small step could Vandana try with the group?
qa.a: Vandana could start with something low-risk, like saying 'I'd actually like the museum', and notice whether real friends stay.

qa.q: How might the new boy feel if he heard the laughter?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and isolated, with no idea that at least one person laughing felt sick about it.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager admits laughing at disliked jokes and agreeing against a personal view out of fear of losing the group.

passage: Okay, so the topic this week is "times you weren't yourself." I'm Anjali, Class 12, and mine is basically all of Class 10. My group, Joseph, Nikhil and the others, had strong opinions on everything. If Joseph said a film was rubbish, I said it was rubbish, even though I'd loved it. When Nikhil made jokes about girls who "try too hard" in class, I laughed, and then I'd go home and do my homework in secret, because I was a girl who tried hard. The worst part was that I believed I had no choice. If I disagreed, maybe they'd drop me. It took a whole year, and one friend outside the group, before I tried saying "I actually liked it" about a film. Joseph shrugged and said, "Fair." That was it.

qa.q: What did Joseph say when Anjali finally said 'I actually liked it'?
qa.a: Joseph shrugged and said, "Fair."

qa.q: Why did Anjali laugh at Nikhil's jokes and then do homework in secret?
qa.a: She feared being dropped by the group, so she hid the part of herself that tried hard in class, even though the jokes hurt.

qa.q: What turning point does Anjali describe, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Saying 'I actually liked it' about a film was a small, safe test; Joseph's easy 'Fair' showed disagreeing didn't mean losing friends.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen Anjali's year of agreeing?
qa.a: Joseph may never have noticed, or may have assumed she truly agreed, which shows how much of the pressure lived in Anjali's fear.

grounding: On a school podcast, a teenager recalls a year of agreeing with friends and laughing at hurtful jokes out of fear of rejection.

passage: I'm Preeti, and I've known Jagdish since Class 3. On his own he's the kindest person, the kind who helps the watchman's son with maths after school. But around the cricket boys he's different. Yesterday at the bus stop, one of them made a joke about the watchman's son's torn shoes. Everyone laughed. Jagdish laughed too, a beat late, and then looked at the ground. When they said the new rule about phones in class was "dumb", Jagdish agreed loudly, even though last week he told me he thought it was fair. I don't know what he really thinks anymore. I don't think he knows either. He just watches their faces before he speaks.

qa.q: What did one of the cricket boys joke about at the bus stop?
qa.a: The watchman's son's torn shoes.

qa.q: What does Jagdish laughing 'a beat late' and looking at the ground suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he didn't find the joke funny and felt uneasy, but laughed so he wouldn't stand out from the group.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try the next time the group mocks someone?
qa.a: He could stay quiet instead of laughing, or say 'Leave it, yaar', and find that one small step doesn't have to cost him the group.

qa.q: How might the watchman's son feel if he knew Jagdish laughed?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and confused, since Jagdish is the one who helps him with maths after school.

grounding: A longtime friend watches a teenage boy laugh at jokes he dislikes and echo the group against his own view.

passage:
Monday: At lunch, Baljeet's group was mocking the new boy's accent. Lokesh didn't find it funny; his own cousin talked just like that. He laughed anyway, loudest of all, and checked Baljeet's face to see if it had been enough.
Wednesday: The group decided the school play was 'for losers'. Lokesh had secretly signed up. When Baljeet asked, 'You're not doing that, right?' he said, 'Obviously not,' and crossed his name off the list after school. His stomach hurt all evening.
Saturday: At the cricket ground, Baljeet made another joke about the new boy, Aniket, who was fielding nearby. Lokesh laughed on cue. Then he saw Aniket's face. Lokesh stopped laughing. He didn't say anything. But he didn't laugh again, and he noticed he could breathe a little easier.

qa.q: What did Lokesh cross off after school on Wednesday?
qa.a: His name, from the school play list.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh laugh loudest at a joke he didn't find funny?
qa.a: He feared being left out of Baljeet's group; laughing loudly and checking Baljeet's face was a way to prove he belonged, even against his own feelings.

qa.q: What was the small turning point on Saturday, and what could Lokesh do next?
qa.a: Seeing Aniket's face and stopping laughing; next, Lokesh could put his name back on the play list or quietly say hello to Aniket, choosing his own view over the group's.

qa.q: What might Aniket notice when Lokesh stops laughing?
qa.a: Aniket may notice that at least one person in the group isn't joining in, a small sign that he isn't completely alone.

grounding: A teenager laughs at jokes he dislikes and drops a play he wanted because the group's approval feels more important than his own view.

passage:
Karthik, I saw you nodding along when your friends said that thing about the girl in your class. You didn't look like you agreed. Let me tell you something from my school days.
At fifteen, in Mangaluru, I was in the group everyone wanted to be in. To stay in, I agreed with everything. They said the science fair was nerdy, so I said it too, though I loved it. They made fun of Reshma's weight, and I laughed, and then I went home and felt sick.
The worst part was that I stopped knowing what I actually thought. I'd wait to hear what they said first.
One day Reshma asked me, 'Sabina, do you even have your own opinion?' I had no answer.
It took me years to get my own voice back, beta. Don't hand yours over so cheaply.

qa.q: What did young Sabina's group say about the science fair?
qa.a: That it was nerdy.

qa.q: Why did young Sabina laugh at the jokes about Reshma and then feel sick?
qa.a: Sabina feared losing a place in the group, so laughed along; but it went against Sabina's own feelings, which came out as guilt at home.

qa.q: What choice is Sabina hoping Karthik will make?
qa.a: To stop nodding along when Karthik disagrees and to hold on to Karthik's own view even if the group frowns, before losing track of it.

qa.q: What might Reshma's question have been like from Reshma's side?
qa.a: Reshma, the target of the jokes, may have been hurt and frustrated, wanting to know whether Sabina really believed them or was only following.

grounding: An elder recalls agreeing with a popular group against their own view and laughing at cruel jokes out of fear of rejection.

passage:
Dear Ira,
You asked how the new friends are. They're fun, mostly. Popular, too. I sit with them at lunch now.
But something's bugging me. Yesterday Neil made fun of Sameer's lunch, the upma his grandmother packs every day. He called it 'wet sand' and everyone laughed. I laughed too. I actually like upma. My Nani makes it. But I laughed louder than anyone, because I didn't want them to look at me the way they looked at Sameer.
Then Neil said the new history teacher is useless, and I agreed, even though I think she's the best one we've got.
I keep saying yes to everything they say. It's like I'm scared that if I disagree once, I'll be back to sitting alone. Is that stupid?
Write back.
Akash

qa.q: What does Sameer's grandmother pack every day?
qa.a: She packs upma every day.

qa.q: Why did Akash laugh louder than anyone?
qa.a: Akash was afraid of being rejected and ending up like Sameer, so pleasing the group mattered more than Akash's own view.

qa.q: What small step could Akash take to be more honest with the group?
qa.a: Akash could stop laughing at jokes that feel wrong, or quietly say upma is good, starting with one small disagreement.

qa.q: How might Sameer feel when everyone laughs at his lunch?
qa.a: Sameer would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, especially about food his grandmother makes for him.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager admits laughing at jokes they dislike and agreeing against their own view, out of fear of the group's rejection.

passage: Vasudha, you want to know why I called that film 'trash' at lunch when I told you last week it was the best thing I'd seen all year? Honestly? Because Karan said it first, and then everyone agreed, and I felt my mouth open and 'yeah, total trash' came out. I didn't even decide. It just came out. Same on Friday, when they decided to bunk the physics practical. I like physics practicals. I went with them anyway and sat behind the canteen feeling stupid. I think I'm scared that if I say 'actually, I liked it', they'll look at me the way they looked at the new boy when he said he doesn't watch cricket. As if he'd stopped existing. So I say yes. To everything. I'm Varun, and apparently I have no opinions anymore. Isn't that funny?

qa.q: What did Varun say about the film at lunch?
qa.a: He said, 'Yeah, total trash.'

qa.q: Why does Varun say yes to everything the group decides?
qa.a: He is afraid of being rejected and treated as if he'd stopped existing, like the new boy, so the group's approval matters more than his own views.

qa.q: What could Varun try next time the group disagrees with him?
qa.a: He could say one small honest thing, like 'I liked it', and see that disagreeing doesn't have to mean rejection.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel hearing Varun called the film trash?
qa.a: Vasudha might feel confused and a little let down, since he had told her it was the best film he'd seen all year.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend how fear of rejection makes him echo the group, trashing a film he loved and skipping a class he enjoys.

passage:
Vandana, you told me you laughed at the joke about the new girl even though it made you feel sick. Let me, your Alka Maasi, tell you about me at fifteen.
In Jaipur, there was a group of girls I badly wanted to belong to. When they said a film was stupid, I said it was stupid, though I had loved it. When they made fun of a girl's oiled plait, I laughed loudest.
One night I went home and cried, because that girl was my neighbour, and she used to share her mangoes with me.
The next day I didn't laugh. I just stayed quiet. The group noticed. It was frightening. For a week I thought they'd drop me.
They didn't, not completely. And I got a little bit of myself back.

qa.q: What did the group make fun of?
qa.a: They made fun of a girl's oiled plait.

qa.q: Why did young Alka laugh loudest at the joke?
qa.a: She was afraid of being rejected by the group, so their approval mattered more to her than her own feelings.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Alka make a different choice?
qa.a: The next day, when she stayed quiet instead of laughing, risking the group's approval.

qa.q: How might the neighbour girl have felt hearing Alka laugh?
qa.a: The neighbour probably felt hurt and betrayed, since Alka was someone she shared mangoes with.

grounding: The aunt's memory shows a teenager agreeing with friends and laughing at jokes she disliked because the group's approval felt more important than herself.

passage:
The school trip bus to Mahabaleshwar was stuck in a four-hour traffic jam, and the back seats had turned into a stage. Damini, the loudest in their group, was rating everyone's outfits out of ten.
“Chetan, agree, na? Priyanka's jacket is a disaster.”
Chetan actually liked the jacket. It was the same colour as his mother's favourite shawl. “Total disaster,” he said, and everyone laughed.
Damini did a mocking voice of a teacher. Chetan thought it was mean. He laughed anyway, a beat too late.
By the third hour, his jaw ached from fake smiling. Priyanka was sitting two seats ahead, very still, earphones in but no music playing.
Chetan looked out at the fog. He had agreed with everything for three hours. He wasn't sure what he actually thought about anything anymore.

qa.q: How long was the traffic jam?
qa.a: It was a four-hour traffic jam.

qa.q: Why did Chetan call the jacket a disaster when he liked it?
qa.a: He was afraid of being left out of Damini's group, so their approval felt more important than his own view.

qa.q: What could Chetan try the next time Damini starts rating people?
qa.a: He could stay quiet or say something simple like “I like it, actually,” keeping some of his own view without starting a fight.

qa.q: What might it be like for Priyanka sitting two seats ahead?
qa.a: Priyanka probably feels humiliated and hurt, pretending to listen to music so no one sees her upset.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager on a long, stuck bus agreeing with friends and laughing at jokes he dislikes because the group's approval feels more important.

passage:
After the interschool football match in Chennai, Suraj's friends were at the juice shop, going over the game.
“The referee was blind,” said Rakesh. “Totally biased.”
Suraj had thought the referee was fair. The penalty was a real foul; he'd seen it clearly. But everyone was nodding.
“Totally biased,” he said.
Then Rakesh started imitating the way Rekha, the girl who scored the other team's goal, celebrated. Everyone laughed. Suraj thought her celebration had been brilliant. He laughed too, because the table was laughing.
On the way home, he felt tired, as though he'd carried something heavy. At the signal, a boy on a cycle did the same celebration, joyfully. Suraj smiled, a real smile this time, and felt a sting of shame about the juice shop.

qa.q: What did Rakesh say about the referee?
qa.a: He said the referee was blind and totally biased.

qa.q: Why did Suraj agree the referee was biased?
qa.a: He was afraid of standing apart from his friends, so their approval felt more important than what he had seen.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next time his friends mock someone?
qa.a: He could simply not laugh, or say he thought Rekha's celebration was great, keeping hold of his own view.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel if she knew the boys were mocking her celebration?
qa.a: Rekha would probably feel hurt and belittled after a moment she was proud of.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager agreeing with friends against his own view and laughing at mockery he dislikes because group approval feels more important.

passage:
I'm Tushar, and the thing I still think about from Class 10 is the trip vote. Our class could choose between a science museum and a water park. I love museums. I had even read about the planetarium show.
Urmila, who basically ran our group, said, "Museum is for kids." Everyone nodded. When the teacher asked for hands, I watched the others first. Water park. My hand went up with theirs.
At the water park I stood in queues and pretended to be excited. That evening Urmila posted our group photo with the caption "best day ever 🎉". I liked it within a minute.
What bothers me is not the water park. It's that I didn't even pause. My hand knew what the group wanted before I checked what I wanted.

qa.q: What were the two options for the class trip?
qa.a: The options were a science museum and a water park.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel at the water park, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tushar felt uncomfortable and fake, standing in queues and pretending to be excited while really wanting the museum.

qa.q: What could Tushar try the next time a group vote comes up?
qa.a: Tushar could decide privately before looking at others' hands, maybe even writing the choice down, so the answer comes from Tushar's own view.

qa.q: How might Urmila see the trip vote?
qa.a: Urmila probably thinks everyone agreed happily, without knowing that at least one hand went up only to fit in.

grounding: It shows a teenager voting with friends against their own wish and pretending to enjoy it because the group's approval matters more than their own view.

passage:
Coach's notes, U-16 hockey — Sarita
Friday: Jyoti usually speaks up at practice. Today the senior girls were talking about the new player, Kiran, who just moved from Manipur. Mahi said, "Her accent is so funny," and copied it. The group laughed. Jyoti laughed too, though her face tightened.
After drills, the girls voted informally on whether Kiran should join their warm-up circle. Jyoti said no with the others. Then she went and sat on the bench alone, tying and retying her laces.
I spoke to Jyoti afterwards. She said, "If I'm the only one who says yes, they'll leave me out next." She looked close to tears.
Next steps: I have told the team that warm-up circles are open to everyone, starting Monday. I will talk to Kiran myself tomorrow and check with Jyoti again next week.

qa.q: What did Mahi say about Kiran?
qa.a: Mahi said, "Her accent is so funny," and copied it.

qa.q: What was Jyoti afraid of when she voted no with the others?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she said yes alone, the group would leave her out next, and she felt close to tears because it went against what she really thought.

qa.q: How did the coach support the team, and what else could help?
qa.a: The coach opened warm-up circles to everyone and planned to check with Kiran and Jyoti; Jyoti could also practise one calm line to say when she disagrees.

qa.q: What is it like for Kiran to be new while the group laughs?
qa.a: Kiran, just moved from Manipur, is likely to feel lonely and unwelcome, shut out of the warm-up circle by girls she barely knows.

grounding: It shows, through a coach's note, a teenager laughing at a joke she dislikes and voting with the group because she fears rejection.

passage:
Diwali break, day 3

Went to Madhuri's for the card party. Seven of us.
Madhuri said the new girl, Esther, "thinks she's so smart" because she answers in class. Everyone agreed. I agreed. I actually like Esther. She lent me her notes when I was sick.
Then the joke about Esther's accent. Everyone laughed. I laughed. It wasn't even funny. My face hurt from laughing at things that weren't funny.
Madhuri asked if the movie we saw last week was boring and I said "so boring", and I LOVED that movie. I cried at the end. Why did I say that?
I think if I say one wrong thing, they'll look at each other the way they look at Esther. And then I'll be the one they talk about at the next party.
Tomorrow Esther's coming to our block for the rangoli. I don't know how to look at her.

Parveen

qa.q: What did Parveen say about last week's movie?
qa.a: "So boring", even though Parveen loved it and cried at the end.

qa.q: Why does Parveen agree and laugh against Parveen's own view?
qa.a: Parveen is afraid of rejection; one wrong word might bring the look the group gives Esther, so their approval feels more important than being honest.

qa.q: What small step could Parveen take?
qa.a: Parveen could skip laughing at the next mean joke, or quietly say "I liked the movie", and be friendly to Esther at the rangoli tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Esther feel if she heard about the party?
qa.a: Esther, who lent Parveen her notes, would likely feel hurt and betrayed to learn she was mocked, especially by someone she helped.

grounding: A teenager agrees with friends against the narrator's own view and laughs at jokes the narrator dislikes, out of fear of rejection.
